title: KB article drafts (batch 1) — Known-issues sprint (Workarounds + escalation criteria)
content:
Doc purpose
- Rough drafts for first set of workaround KB articles.
- Goal: copy/paste-ready for Support macros + linkable from Support workflows.
- IMPORTANT: keep customer names, contract details, internal hostnames, and employee-only dashboards out of final published versions.

House style (draft guidance)
- Start with “Symptoms” + “Impact” so Support can confirm it’s the same issue in <2 minutes.
- Always include:
  (1) Affected tiers/regions/models (even if “unknown/varies”),
  (2) Quick checks for Support,
  (3) Workaround steps with exact settings + examples,
  (4) “When to escalate” with crisp triggers and required artifacts.
- “Temporary workaround” must be labeled as temporary.

========================================
DRAFT 1 — Streaming timeouts / reconnect issues
Working title: Streaming responses reset / disconnect mid-generation (HTTP stream reset, truncated output)
Owner: Wei Chen
Reviewer(s): Owen Phillips (Support), Rafael Mendes (SRE)
Status: Draft (needs SRE validation)

Summary
Some clients see streaming responses disconnect mid-generation. This can present as a truncated response, a client-side timeout, or a connection reset.

Symptoms
- Stream ends unexpectedly before model completes output.
- Client logs show one of:
  - “connection reset by peer”
  - “stream closed” / “unexpected EOF”
  - read timeout during streaming
- Higher frequency behind certain proxies / long-lived connections.

Impact
- Partial/truncated outputs.
- Increased retries from client may increase token usage.
- Some apps interpret disconnect as “model failed”.

Likely causes (high-level)
- Network/proxy timeout closing long-lived connections.
- Client-side timeout too low for long generations.
- HTTP/2 edge-case handling (varies by environment).

Affected
- Tier: Hosted API (most common), can also affect Dedicated depending on customer networking/proxies.
- Regions: varies (track if clustered by region; do not speculate publicly).
- Models: any streaming-capable model.

Quick checks (Support)
1) Confirm endpoint + SDK + streaming mode
   - endpoint: /chat/completions (or equivalent)
   - streaming: true
   - SDK version
2) Ask for request IDs around the failure window (2–5 examples).
3) Ask customer if behind a proxy/load balancer (Cloudflare, ALB, Nginx, corporate proxy, etc.).
4) Confirm approximate duration before disconnect (e.g., “~60s” or “~120s”).

Workarounds (temporary)
A) Increase client-side timeouts
- Set read/response timeout to tolerate longer generation + network jitter.
- Recommended starting point (guidance; adjust per app):
  - connect timeout: 10s
  - read timeout: 300s (5 min) for streaming
  - overall request timeout: >= max expected generation time

[PLACEHOLDER: Python SDK example snippet]
- TODO (Wei): add Python snippet aligning with redwood-sdk-python/pr-921

[PLACEHOLDER: TypeScript example snippet]
- TODO: add TS snippet (confirm naming)

B) Implement safe retry/backoff for stream disconnects
- If a stream disconnect occurs, retry with exponential backoff.
- If your app can tolerate duplicates, use idempotency keys / request correlation so you can detect duplicate completions.
- Do NOT retry indefinitely; cap retries.

Suggested retry policy (starting point)
- max retries: 2
- backoff: 250ms, 1s (+ jitter)
- retry on: transient network errors, 502/503/504, stream disconnect
- do not retry on: 400 invalid request, auth errors

C) If feasible, test disabling HTTP/2 (environment-dependent)
- Some client stacks/proxies handle HTTP/1.1 streaming more reliably.
- Guidance: test in a controlled environment first.

[REVIEW (Rafael/SRE)]: Confirm we want to mention HTTP/2 at all in the public KB, or keep as “If using HTTP/2 via proxy, try HTTP/1.1” without implying a platform bug.

D) Reduce generation length / stream duration
- For very long generations, consider:
  - lowering max_output_tokens
  - chunking tasks (multi-call)
  - summarizing intermediate results

What to collect (Support ask)
- 3–5 request IDs where streaming disconnect occurs
- Region
- Model
- SDK + version
- Client environment: language/runtime + proxy/LB details
- Approx time-to-disconnect
- Whether customer sees the issue on a direct connection (bypassing proxy)

[PLACEHOLDER: Screenshot]
- “Client log snippet showing disconnect + timestamps (redact secrets)”

When to escalate
Escalate to SRE/on-call if any of the following:
- Many customers affected or sudden increase in volume (possible regional degradation)
- Reproducible across environments, including direct connection without customer proxy
- Error rate spike correlated in platform metrics (Support to check internal dashboards)
- Customer is Dedicated/Enterprise + impact is P0/P1 per severity rubric

Internal notes (remove before publish)
- Related tickets: SUP-1842, SUP-1854
- Engineering follow-ups: ENG-4822 (error messaging), SDK docs: ENG-4827

DRAFT 2 — 429 quota mismatch / rate-limit header confusion
Working title: Unexpected 429s and confusing rate-limit headers (quota vs rate limiting)
Owner: Wei Chen
Reviewer(s): Ethan Park (Platform), Priya Shah (Support)
Status: Draft

Summary
Customers may see 429 responses that appear inconsistent with their expected quota/limits, and rate-limit headers may be misinterpreted.

Symptoms
- Increased 429 responses after SDK upgrade or config change.
- Customer sees headers such as remaining/reset values that don’t match expected usage.
- Confusion between “rate limit exceeded” vs “quota exceeded”.

Impact
- Requests fail under load.
- Customers throttle incorrectly (over-throttle or under-throttle).

Key concept
- “Quota” is an account-level allowance over a billing period or contract window.
- “Rate limit” is a short-window protection to keep systems stable (per minute/second, per key, etc.).
- 429 may be returned for either scenario depending on endpoint and enforcement layer.

Quick checks (Support)
1) Confirm which limit is hit:
   - Ask for full response headers (redact auth).
   - Ask for timestamps + approximate QPS / TPM.
2) Confirm SDK version and whether customer uses custom retry logic.
3) Confirm whether traffic is bursty (spikes) vs steady.
4) Ask if multiple services share the same API key.

Common causes
- Burst traffic exceeding short-window rate limits.
- Retries without backoff multiplying effective request rate.
- Multiple deployments sharing a key.
- SDK default retry settings changed between versions.

Workarounds
A) Implement client-side throttling aligned to headers
- Respect the provided rate-limit headers.
- If headers are absent/unclear, implement conservative backoff on 429.

Suggested approach
- On 429:
  - wait until reset time if provided
  - else exponential backoff with jitter
  - cap concurrency

B) Reduce request burstiness
- Queue requests and smooth spikes.
- Avoid simultaneous warm-start bursts during deploys.

C) Validate account limits with Support (for quota concerns)
- Support can confirm configured account limits and recent usage patterns.

[REVIEW (Ethan/Platform)]: confirm phrasing so we don’t promise Support can instantly change limits; say “Support can confirm current limits and route requests for changes.”

Artifacts to request
- 2–3 example responses including:
  - status code
  - response headers
  - timestamp
  - request ID(s)
- Region + endpoint
- SDK version

[PLACEHOLDER: Screenshot]
- “Example 429 response headers (sanitized)”

When to escalate
- Escalate to Platform if:
  - headers appear inconsistent across identical calls, or
  - customer provides evidence of misclassification (e.g., quota remaining but 429)
- Escalate if multiple customers report same pattern after a platform release.

Internal notes (remove before publish)
- Related: SUP-1843, SUP-1855
- Fix in flight: ENG-4825 / redwood PR-19322

DRAFT 3 — Dedicated autoscaling oscillation (latency spikes)
Working title: Dedicated autoscaling oscillation causing latency spikes / instability
Owner: Kira Thompson
Reviewer(s): Sean Gallagher (SRE), Allison Grant (Observability)
Status: Draft (needs screenshots + “safe” dashboard language)

Summary
On Dedicated pools, aggressive scaling policies can cause replica churn (scale up/down repeatedly). This can lead to latency spikes, cold starts, and inconsistent throughput.

Symptoms
- Latency spikes that correlate with frequent scaling events.
- Throughput/queue depth sawtooth pattern.
- Increased tail latency after scale-down events.

Impact
- p95/p99 latency regressions.
- Higher error rates if queues overflow.
- Customer sees inconsistent performance during peak load.

Affected
- Tier: Dedicated
- Regions: any
- Models: most noticeable for larger models or workloads sensitive to warm cache.

Quick checks (Support/CS)
- Ask if the customer recently changed:
  - min replicas / max replicas
  - scale-down cooldown
  - target utilization
- Check whether traffic pattern is spiky (batch jobs) vs smooth.

Workarounds (configuration knobs)
A) Increase minimum replicas
- Set min replicas high enough to handle baseline traffic without scaling.
- Benefit: reduces cold starts.

B) Increase scale-down cooldown / stabilization window
- Prevent scale-down too quickly after a transient spike.
- Typical starting point: 10–20 minutes cooldown (depends on workload).

C) Reduce scaling aggressiveness
- Use smaller scaling increments.
- Avoid policies that react to very short windows.

D) (If available) enable “stability guardrail” setting
- If the platform supports a guardrail mode, enable it.

[REVIEW (Sean/SRE)]: confirm what’s GA vs internal-only. We should not mention features customers can’t access.

What to collect
- Workload pattern: peak QPS/TPM + spike behavior
- Current autoscaling config values
- Time window of latency spikes

[PLACEHOLDER: Screenshot]
- “Dedicated pool autoscaling events timeline (redacted)”

When to escalate
Escalate to SRE/Capacity when:
- Latency spikes persist even with conservative scaling settings
- Customer is at risk of breaching their SLA/SLO commitments
- Customer requests a capacity review or reserved headroom

DRAFT 4 — Private installer upgrade stuck (migrations)
Working title: Private deployment upgrade stuck at “migrations” (installer upgrade failure)
Owner: Kira Thompson
Reviewer(s): Priya Natarajan (Platform), Naomi Feldman (Security/compliance)
Status: Draft (needs validation for “safe rollback” language)

Summary
Private deployments may encounter upgrade failures where the installer appears stuck during migrations. This is often due to resource constraints, job failures, or environment-specific cluster conditions.

Symptoms
- Upgrade progress does not advance for extended period during “migrations” step.
- Installer output shows repeated retry attempts.
- Kubernetes job pods crashloop or remain pending.

Impact
- Upgrade blocked.
- Risk of partial upgrade state if interrupted incorrectly.

Before you start (safety)
- If the deployment is production: coordinate a maintenance window if possible.
- Do not delete resources unless instructed; collect diagnostics first.

Quick checks
- Confirm cluster health:
  - node capacity available
  - pending pods
  - recent cluster events
- Confirm installer version and previous version.

Workarounds / mitigation steps
A) Collect diagnostics bundle
- Generate the installer diagnostics bundle if available.

[PLACEHOLDER: Command / UI steps]
- TODO: update after ENG-4828 / private-installer PR-566 is merged

B) Check migration job status
- Identify migration job/pod and capture logs.

[PLACEHOLDER: Sanitized “kubectl logs …” example]
- (Include redaction note: tokens, endpoints, secrets must be removed)

C) Safe rollback guidance (high-level)
- If rollback is supported, follow documented rollback procedure.
- If rollback is not supported in your version, stop and escalate.

[REVIEW (Naomi/Security)]: ensure we do not instruct actions that could cause data loss; keep rollback guidance minimal and gated behind escalation if unclear.

Artifacts to request (Support)
- Installer logs (sanitized)
- Cluster events for the upgrade window
- Versions: installer + platform
- Any custom configuration overlays

When to escalate
Escalate to Private Deployments/Platform when:
- Upgrade remains stuck >30 minutes with no progress AND logs indicate repeated failures
- Any sign of data migration errors
- Customer is air-gapped or highly regulated (avoid back-and-forth; page the right owners)

DRAFT 5 — Audit log delivery latency (delayed audit logs)
Working title: Audit logs delayed / delivery latency higher than expected
Owner: Kira Thompson
Reviewer(s): Allison Grant (Observability), Rachel Kim (Enterprise CS)
Status: Draft

Summary
Audit logs may be delivered with a delay. This can be expected under certain conditions, but sustained or extreme delays may indicate pipeline backlog.

Symptoms
- Customer reports audit logs arriving late (e.g., >30 minutes after events).
- Gaps or bursts in delivered audit log stream.

Impact
- Compliance workflows delayed.
- Monitoring/alerting systems may be less effective.

Expected behavior (set expectations carefully)
- Audit logs are delivered asynchronously.
- Short delays may occur during transient load.

[REVIEW (Rachel/CS)]: we need exact SLO language per tier and what we can commit to publicly. Avoid numbers unless they match enterprise docs.

Quick checks (Support)
1) Confirm integration method (webhook/export/etc.)
2) Confirm the “event time” vs “delivery time” the customer is measuring.
3) Ask for a sample of:
   - event timestamp
   - delivery timestamp
   - region

Workarounds (temporary)
A) Increase consumer retry window / tolerance
- Ensure the customer’s ingestion system can handle delayed delivery and retries.

B) Prefer batch export window if supported
- If near-real-time isn’t required, batch export reduces sensitivity to short backlogs.

C) If customer alerts depend on audit logs, adjust alert thresholds temporarily
- Move from “immediate” to “delayed acceptable window” where appropriate.

Artifacts to request
- Time range of issue
- Sample delayed events (IDs/timestamps)
- Delivery method

[PLACEHOLDER: Screenshot]
- “Audit log delivery timeline view (customer-safe)”

When to escalate
Escalate to SRE/Platform if:
- Delay exceeds agreed expectations for tier
- Multiple customers reporting the same pattern
- Support confirms pipeline backlog via internal metrics

Internal notes (remove before publish)
- Related: SUP-1846
- Engineering follow-up: ENG-4824 / observability-pack PR-711

========================================
Publishing checklist (for each article)
Owner: Elliot / Docs team

Pre-publish
[ ] Title matches naming convention ("Workaround: <symptom>")
[ ] No customer names, no internal hostnames, no contract terms, no internal-only links
[ ] “Affected tiers/regions/models” included (or “unknown” explicitly stated)
[ ] “Workaround” is copy/paste-ready; clearly marked temporary if temporary
[ ] “When to escalate” includes required artifacts (request IDs, region, model, SDK)
[ ] Support macro snippet prepared (or linked) and matches article language
[ ] SRE/Platform reviewer sign-off for technical accuracy
[ ] CS/Legal sign-off if SLA/SLO wording is included

Post-publish
[ ] Add to Known Issues index with tags + last-updated date
[ ] Cross-link from Support intake checklist + Jira automation prompt
[ ] Announce in #support with one-paragraph summary + link
[ ] Add to docs-site nav if needed (tracked via ENG-4826)

Metrics to watch (post-sprint)
- Ticket deflection (repeat ticket rate for each issue)
- Time-to-triage (from ticket created to correct classification)
- Time-to-mitigation (customer receiving actionable workaround)
